judge.explanation: The sentence restates the paper's own central finding, almost in its own words. The abstract says that 'in no instance' did the authors observe systematic evidence of an increase in conspiracism. This covers the United States (Study 1: 46 specific theories, some tracked over up to 55 years; Studies 3-4: perceived conspirators and conspiracy thinking, 2012-2021) and six European countries (Study 2: Germany, Great Britain, Italy, Poland, Portugal, Sweden, 2016 vs 2018). In Study 2, only 1 of 35 comparisons rose significantly and 7 fell. Direction, the number of countries and the populations all match, and the sentence makes no causal claim. 'No systematic evidence' is accurate even though the paper reports a few significant increases (7 of 46 in Study 1; 13 of 52 across Studies 1-2), because the authors themselves judge these insufficient. 'Contrary to this impression' matches the paper's framing against the popular belief that conspiracism is rising. Context only, not an error: the European test covers six theories over two years, and the authors say they cannot rule out increases in other beliefs or other countries; the sentence does not claim more than this.

judge.explanation: Only the OpenAlex abstract of Goertzel (1994) is available (no open-access full text). The manuscript attributes to Goertzel the argument that conspiracy theories offer people simple explanations for events that are otherwise hard to understand. The abstract contains nothing of the kind: it reports a survey of 348 New Jersey residents and correlations of conspiracy belief with anomia, lack of interpersonal trust, employment insecurity, race/ethnicity and age, plus the finding that belief in one conspiracy goes with belief in others. A search of the abstract for 'simple', 'explanation', 'understand', 'complex', 'event', 'sense' and related terms found no match. The abstract neither supports nor contradicts the attributed argument, which may appear in the paper's discussion, so the claim cannot be settled from the available text. No source in the manuscript's reference list makes this argument as its own: the candidates helper and a search of all source texts found only secondary summaries (e.g. vanprooijen2023: 'Conspiracy theories help people understand their social environment (Douglas et al., 2019; Van Prooijen, 2020)'; imhoff2020 on events of magnitude begging explanation, citing Leman & Cinnirella, 2007), which are about sense-making or control rather than 'simple explanations' and are attributed to other works.

source_summary.main_results: Paranoia predicted higher endorsement overall (estimate 0.83, 95% CI 0.72-0.93). Incidental-harm and society-targeted items were endorsed more overall. More paranoid participants were relatively more likely to endorse intentional-harm and self-referential items; the self-referential effect is called marginal. In the network analysis endorsement clustered mainly by intentionality, and the edge from paranoia to intentional/self items was stronger than the edge to intentional/society items. Participants endorsed items they thought similar others endorsed, and paranoia did not weaken this effect. There are no data on interventions to reduce conspiracy beliefs.
